1.q: וְ⁠יָצָ֥א חֹ֖טֶר מִ⁠גֵּ֣זַע יִשָׁ֑י וְ⁠נֵ֖צֶר מִ⁠שָּׁרָשָׁ֥י⁠ו יִפְרֶֽה
1.note: These two phrases **a shoot will come out from the stump of Jesse** and **a branch from his roots will bear fruit** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [A descendant of Jesse will rise up and accomplish great things]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the dynasty of Jesse were a tree stump and a future descendant were **a shoot** growing from it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And a descendant of Jesse will come forth]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if a future descendant of Jesse were **a branch from his roots** that would **bear fruit**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a descendant of his will accomplish great things]
The pronoun **his** refers to Jesse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Jesse’s roots]

2.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the Spirit of Yahweh were a person who could physically **rest on** someone, meaning the Spirit would remain with him permanently. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the Spirit of Yahweh will remain with him]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe the **Spirit** that comes from **Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the Spirit that comes from Yahweh]

The pronoun **him** refers to the Messiah, the descendant of Jesse described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on this descendant of Jesse]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [being wise and having understanding]

The terms **wisdom** and **understanding** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great wisdom]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **counsel** and **might**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [good advice and strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [knowing Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fear**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the spirit of revering Yahweh]

3.note: Isaiah is using **by the sight of his eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “by what is seeable.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by what his eyes see]

Here, **the sight of his eyes** represents outward appearance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by what he sees]

Isaiah is using **by the hearing of his ears** as a common expression of the culture to mean “by what is seeable.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by what his ears hear]

Here, **the hearing of his ears** represents what others report to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by what others report to him]

3.q: וַ⁠הֲרִיח֖⁠וֹ בְּ⁠יִרְאַ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹֽא־לְ⁠מַרְאֵ֤ה עֵינָי⁠ו֙ יִשְׁפּ֔וֹט וְ⁠לֹֽא־לְ⁠מִשְׁמַ֥ע אָזְנָ֖י⁠ו יוֹכִֽיחַ
3.note: The pronouns **he** and **his** refer to the Messiah, the descendant of Jesse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Messiah’s breathing will be in the fear of Yahweh, and the Messiah will not judge by the sight of his own eyes, and he will not decide by the hearing of his own ears]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fear**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will be in fearing Yahweh]

4.note: Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between what the Messiah will not do, that is, judge by outward appearance, and what he will do, that is, judge with righteousness. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [rather, he will judge]

Isaiah is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those in need]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uprightness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [uprightly]

Isaiah is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for poor people of the earth]

4.q: וְ⁠הִֽכָּה אֶ֨רֶץ֙ בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣בֶט פִּ֔י⁠ו וּ⁠בְ⁠ר֥וּחַ שְׂפָתָ֖י⁠ו יָמִ֥ית רָשָֽׁע
4.note: Isaiah is using the expressions **his mouth** and **the breath of his lips** to represent what this new king will say by using his mouth, breath, and lips. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will strike the earth with the rod of his words, yes, by what he says, he will kill the wicked]

Isaiah is speaking as if what this king will say would be a **rod** with which he would **strike** the people of the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will punish the earth by what he says] or [And he will give commands to punish the earth]

Isaiah is using the term **earth** to represent the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth]

Isaiah is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and he will give orders to execute people who are wicked]

5.q: וְ⁠הָ֥יָה צֶ֖דֶק אֵז֣וֹר מָתְנָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠הָ⁠אֱמוּנָ֖ה אֵז֥וֹר חֲלָצָֽי⁠ו
5.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if **righteousness** and **faithfulness** were **the belt** that equips the Messiah, meaning these qualities will characterize and prepare him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Righteousness will characterize him, and faithfulness will equip him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated this in 11:4. Alternate translation: [what is right]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The implied verb is **will be**, which can be understood from the first clause. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and faithfulness will be the belt of his hips]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his faithful actions]

6.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The implied verb is **will be** or **will stay**, which can be understood from the earlier clauses. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the calf and the young lion and the fatling will be together]

7.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the ox** eats straw as its natural food, so **the lion** will also eat straw instead of meat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the lion will eat straw just as the ox eats straw]

8.note: It can be stated clearly that the baby will be safe because the snake will not bite it. Alternate translation: [A toddler will be safe playing beside the home of a poisonous snake]

8.q: וְ⁠שִֽׁעֲשַׁ֥ע יוֹנֵ֖ק עַל־חֻ֣ר פָּ֑תֶן וְ⁠עַל֙ מְאוּרַ֣ת צִפְעוֹנִ֔י גָּמ֖וּל יָד֥⁠וֹ הָדָֽה
8.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And the nursing child will play over the hole of the adder, indeed, the weaned child will stretch out his hand over the den of the viper]

Unlike a **nursing** child, a **weaned child** is no longer drinking its mother’s milk. If your readers would not be familiar with what a **weaned child** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term, as modeled by the UST.

9.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [text]

Here Isaiah is using the pronoun **They** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will cause harm or destroy] or [No one will be harmed or destroyed]

The implication is that **the mountain of my holiness** refers to Mount Zion, where the temple stands. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on all of Mount Zion, the mountain of my holiness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on all of my holy mountain]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of those who know]

9.q: מָלְאָ֣ה הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ דֵּעָה֙ אֶת־יְהוָ֔ה כַּ⁠מַּ֖יִם לַ⁠יָּ֥ם מְכַסִּֽים
9.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the waters** are completely **covering the sea**, so **the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [everyone on earth will know Yahweh as fully as the waters cover the sea]

10.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **And it will happen** to introduce a new event in the prophecy. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
To translate the phrase **in that day** here and in the rest of this chapter, see how you translated it in [4:1](ta:04).

Here Isaiah is speaking as if a descendant of Jesse were **the root of Jesse**, as though this person were part of a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the offspring of Jesse]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the Messiah were **a banner** that the peoples rally around. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that is standing will be a leader for all the peoples]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the Messiah’s reign were a **resting place**, a place of settled safety and honor. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his reign will be glorious]

10.q: אֵלָ֖י⁠ו גּוֹיִ֣ם יִדְרֹ֑שׁוּ וְ⁠הָיְתָ֥ה מְנֻחָת֖⁠וֹ כָּבֽוֹד
10.note: The pronoun **him** refers to the descendant of Jesse, the Messiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [To this descendant of Jesse the nations will seek, and his resting place will be glory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [glorious]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 11:10.

Here, **his hand** represents the Lord’s power and action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Lord will act with his power]

Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb, **will be left**, and its object, **the remnant**, come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

The expression **who will be left** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whom God kept in Assyria]

Isaiah is using **the coastlands of the sea** as a common expression of the culture to mean distant lands across the sea. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and from the distant lands beyond the sea]

12.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the Lord’s act of gathering his people were **raising a banner** to signal the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will give a signal to the nations]

The expression **the outcast ones** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [those of Israel whom enemies drove out]

The expression **the scattered ones** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the ones of Judah whom enemies had scattered]

Isaiah is using **the four edges of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean every part of the world. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from every part of the earth]

13.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **envy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And Ephraim will cease to envy]

Here, **Ephraim** represents the northern kingdom of Israel, since Ephraim was its most prominent tribe. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the northern kingdom of Israel]

Here, **Judah** represents the southern kingdom, since Judah was its primary tribe. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the southern kingdom]

The expression **will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will stop being hostile]

14.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the reunited people of Israel and Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel and Judah will fly on the shoulder of]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the reunited Israelites attacking the Philistines were birds that **fly on the shoulder** of a hillside, meaning they will swoop down on Philistine territory. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they will swoop down from the heights upon the Philistines]

Isaiah is using **the sons of the east** as a common expression of the culture to mean the peoples who live to the east of Israel. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the peoples who live to the east]

Here, **the sending forth of their hand** represents their power to conquer and control those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will be subject to their power]

Isaiah is using **the sons of Ammon** as a common expression of the culture to mean the Ammonite people. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the Ammonite people]

Here, **their listener** represents those who obey them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their obedient servants]

15.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the gulf of the sea were a **tongue** because of its shape. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the inlet of the Sea of Egypt]

In this context, the term **devote** has the specialized meaning of making something so that it can no longer be used. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will completely destroy]

Here, **he will wave his hand** represents Yahweh using his power to act against the River. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he will use his power to act against the River]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dryness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with his dry wind]

16.note: The expression **who will be left** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who remain]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:11.

The point of this comparison is that just as Yahweh provided a way **for Israel** when they came up **from the land of Egypt**, so he will provide a highway for the remnant of his people returning from Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [for Israel when Yahweh brought them up from the land of Egypt]

16.q: וְ⁠הָיְתָ֣ה מְסִלָּ֔ה לִ⁠שְׁאָ֣ר עַמּ֔⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִשָּׁאֵ֖ר מֵֽ⁠אַשּׁ֑וּר כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר הָֽיְתָה֙ לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּ⁠י֥וֹם עֲלֹת֖⁠וֹ מֵ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם
16.note: The pronoun **his** in **his people** refers to the Lord, while the pronoun **his** in **his coming up** refers to Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant of Yahweh’s people who will be left, as there was for Israel in the day of Israel’s coming up from the land of Egypt]
